# Methods

```{r}
source("./code/not_functions/libraries.R")
```

## Description of the FSSG

The 'Fischwendelschleuse' or FSSG is a fish passage with an adjustable attracting current aimed for all fish species (Fig. \@ref(fig:operation)). This system enables continuous sluice operation and should also accommodate bottom-dwelling fish. It features an individually doped multi-chamber lock system with adjustable current options in both the inflow and outflow chambers. Connections to the water, both above and below the surface, are made using a guide flow opening in line with guideline specifications for optimal findability. The lock doors are dimensioned to match the slot sizes of vertical-slot fish passes.

```{r operation, fig.cap = "Operating principle of the FSSG.", fig.show = "hold", fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
include_graphics(path = "./media/operation.pdf")
```

The fish pass is designed to be as natural as possible via a natural substrate base and upright built (i.e., not rotating) (Fig. \@ref(fig:natuurlijk)). The lock control is adaptable for each lock chamber to suit different target fish species and can be temporarily adjusted for individual fish using a monitoring system. The FSSG lock is compact, suitable for fall heights of 1 to 10 meters, and requires minimal construction. It has few moving parts and simple controls. Currently, the FSSG lock is being designed with diameters of 2 to 5 meters and flow rates of 50 to 500 liters per second. An additional attracting flow of approximately 500 to 2500 liters per second can be realized for both inflow and outflow.

```{r natuurlijk, fig.cap = "The entire fish pass is designed to be as natural as possible via a natural substrate base (left) and upright built (right).", fig.show = "hold", fig.align = "center", out.width = "50%"}
include_graphics(path = c("./media/substraat.jpg", "./media/verticaal.png"))
```

### Underwater connection via the outflow chamber and guide flow opening

The FSSG lock is installed underwater within a custom-designed outflow chamber, which also serves as its foundation (Fig. \@ref(fig:inlet)). This chamber guides fish either ascending to the lock doors or descending to the guide flow opening. To mimic a natural environment, the outflow chamber is filled with base substrate. The system is fine-tuned to the specific water conditions and any operational settings nearby structures such as sluices or hydropower installations might have. This is achieved by designing the underwater guide flow opening with guide walls and bottom connections, and optimizing attracting flow and direction. All these adjustments comply with the fish pass guidelines, similar to vertical slot fish passes.

```{r inlet, fig.cap = "Inlet of the FSSG.", fig.show = "hold", fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
include_graphics(path = "./media/inlet.pdf")
```

A monitoring system near the guide flow opening identifies individual fish, classifies them by species, and adjusts the lock control and attracting flow accordingly. This system also enables statistical recording of fish species and functional monitoring of the FSSG lock.

### Upstream connection via the inflow chamber and guide flow opening

A watertight inflow chamber is installed upstream of the FSSG lock, its height designed to accommodate the normal fluctuations in surface water levels (Fig. \@ref(fig:outlet)). This inflow chamber facilitates the targeted movement of fish, guiding those willing to descend to all lock doors and those ascending to the guide flow opening. To mimic a natural environment, the chamber is filled with base substrate. The guide flow opening can be integrated into the main flow with a base connection and guide wall, enabling a high attracting flow into the inflow chamber. This design ensures the FSSG lock's suitability for fish descent while maintaining low flow velocities in front of the guide flow opening to prevent the unintentional drifting of ascending fish into the driving water.

```{r outlet, fig.cap = "Outlet of the FSSG.", fig.show = "hold", fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
include_graphics(path = "./media/outlet.pdf")
```

In the area of the guide flow opening, a monitoring system records individual fish, assigns them to species, and adjusts the lock control and attracting flow accordingly. This system also allows for the statistical recording of fish species and the functional monitoring of the FSSG lock.

### Continuous multi-chamber lock system

Due to its design, the function of the multi-chamber lock system (Fig. \@ref(fig:locks)) in the FSSG lock cannot be divided into distinct successive phases. Typically, lock systems operate in phases such as swimming in, lifting or lowering, and floating out. In the FSSG lock, these phases can occur simultaneously within the lock chambers, enabling continuous locking without unfavourable dwell times for the fish. The upper and lower water entries into the FSSG lock are through vertically operated, slow-moving lock doors. The adjustable lock current openings in these doors allow them to be perceived as swim-in openings even when closed. When the lock door is opened, it creates a flow rate and speed that meet fish pass guidelines, ensuring clear perception as an ascent or descent route. The duration the valves are open or closed, as well as the time it takes to open and close the valves, can be individually set for each lock chamber. The chambers are completely filled with water, eliminating any gradations or waterfalls. The spiral sole is designed to be non-slip with a substrate thickness of 10 to 30 cm. The dimensions of the lock chambers are in line with the specifications of vertical slot fish pass guidelines.

```{r locks, fig.cap = "Valves of the FSSG.", fig.show = "hold", fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
include_graphics(path = "./media/locks.pdf")
```

Counter-currents are noticeable for fish on the outer diameter, with flow speeds of approximately 0.3 m/s. In the central tube area, the flow speed is low and can be increased with minimal energy. The selectable spiral gradient allows ground-dwelling creatures, such as crabs, to easily navigate through. The lock chamber can be considered a large habitat with reliable bird protection. The central tube enables access via a ladder during lock operation and provides natural lighting. Exposure windows are uniformly sized, and lock doors can be manually opened. Additionally, artificial lighting using LED strips is provided. The central tube is flood-proof and closed at the top with a translucent dome. Waterproof maintenance accesses are installed at the top of the lock system for cleaning and filling with base substrate. Electrical or hydraulically automated devices for the lock doors are also located here, along with a safety railing to prevent falls.

In the event of flooding, all lock doors close simultaneously to minimize contamination with flotsam and sediment. This can also be done during low water phases to avoid additional water losses. If the outside temperature drops below -10 degrees, the spiral lock must be taken out of operation to prevent ice damage. The FSSG lock is emptied in a controlled manner for this purpose.

## Set-up

Only one of the three canals built in the system was used. Prior to the experiments (Fig. \@ref(fig:front)), the lower and upper tanks were slightly modified by installing a metal plate to direct the flow of the lower valve towards the rank. Additionally, possible escape routes from the test tank were closed with a small mesh sized grid. Potential “shelter” areas under the bottom plates of the valve were also closed off.

```{r front, fig.cap = "Front view of the FSSG.", fig.show = "hold", fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
include_graphics(path = "./media/front.pdf")
```

Two HDX PIT antennae (40 mm \* 50 mm) made of copper coil wrapped around graphite bars and connected to permanent readers were installed, each on the front of the upper or lower valve. They were both tuned to have a narrow detection range of approximately 15 cm maximum so that fish would be detected when they cross the valve only – and thus enter the system. Preliminary testing of the system was conducted, assuring the efficiency and detection range of the PIT telemetry set-up.

## Fish experiments

For the experiments of 2023 (exp0) on 5/5/2023 (47 tagged individuals), 8/5/2023 (70 tagged individuals) and 23/5/2023 (49 tagged individuals), a total of 166 individuals of seven different species were used: bleak (*Alburnus alburnus*: 4 individuals), roach (*Rutilus rutilus*: 33 individuals), bream (*Abramis brama*: 12 individuals), gibel carp (*Carassius gibelio*: 6 individuals), carp (*Cyprinus carpio*: 1 individual), white bream (*Blicca bjoerkna*: 100 individuals) and rudd (*Scardinius erythrophthalmus*: 10 individuals). Wild fish, that were caught in the river Yzer, were used  Fish were not re-used for the different experiments. Recapture data was not available which meant that passage efficiency could not be determined accurately. To determine passage efficiency in a sound way at least two measures per fish were needed: Whether a fish entered the system (and moment of entrance preferably) and whether a fish was recaptured (the moment of recapture is less insightful than the moment of entrance as it is the moment that a fish enters a new site of the system (or node, see further) that is of importance). In addition, only limited valve data was available due to an issue of data be overwritten. As such the valves opening values for the upper and lower valves were only available from 23/05/2023 to 26/05/2023. For the experiments of 2024 these issues were resolved.

```{r overzichtexp0}
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')
read.csv("./data/intern/overzichtexp0.csv",sep=";", check.names = F) %>% rename_with(~gsub(".", " ", .x, fixed = TRUE)) %>% kable(caption="Overview of the number of tagged fish per species and per data during the 2023 experiment.")
```

For the experiments of 2024 on 15/5/2023 (exp1), 22/5/2023 (exp2) and 29/5/2023 (exp3) 60, 102 and 124 individuals of ide (*Leuciscus idus*) were used. These fish were bought from a fish farm which utilizes fish culture ponds. If possible, fish used for one experiment were re-used for the next to increase the sampling size and assess the effect of experience. In the second experiment 42 fish were re-used while in the last experiment 88 fish were re-used). Valve data was available for the entire duration of the experiments, albeit at different temporal resolutions (see further). Here it was decided to work with only one species to allow for an acceptable statistical power to draw sound conclusions.

# Read in all pit tag data (exp0, exp1, exp2 and exp3)
dir1<-"./data/extern/pit/"
folders<-list.files(path=dir1)
for (i in 1:length(folders)){
  dir2<-paste0(dir1,folders[i],"/")
  files<-list.files(path=dir2)
  for (j in 1:length(files)){
    dir3<-paste0(dir2,files[j])
    file<-read.table(dir3,header=FALSE,sep='\t')
    file<-as.data.frame(file[substr(file$V1, 0, 1) == "D", ])
    file<-as.data.frame(str_split_fixed(file[,1], "\\s+", 12))[,c(2,3,6)]
    colnames(file)<-c("Date","Time","tag_code")
    file$event_date_time_value<-round_date(as.POSIXct(paste(file$Date,file$Time),format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS",tz="Europe/Brussels"),unit="1 second")
    attr(file$event_date_time_value, "tzone") <- "UTC"
    file<-file %>% dplyr::select(-Date,-Time)
    file$event_site_code_value<-sub("\\s+[^ ]+$", "", files[j])
    if (i==1 & j==1){data=file} else{data=rbind(data,file)}
  }
}
remove(dir1,dir2,dir3,file,folders,files)
data$event_site_code_value=gsub(" ","_",tolower(data$event_site_code_value))
data$antenna_id="01"
data$antenna_group_configuration_value=100
data<-data[startsWith(data$tag_code,"9")==TRUE,]
data<-data[-which(data$tag_code %in% c("900_2280000_228000535717","900_2280\xc9D\xe2LI","900_228000535Y")),]
data$tag_code<-gsub("_","",data$tag_code)
data$event_site_code_value[which(data$event_site_code_value=="vdz_boven")]="upper valve"
data$event_site_code_value[which(data$event_site_code_value=="vdz_onder")]="lower valve"

data$exp<-NA
data$exp[which(format(as.Date(data$event_date_time_value, format="%d/%m/%Y"),"%Y")=="2023")]="exp0"
data$exp[which(data$event_date_time_value>=start.exp1 & data$event_date_time_value<=stop.exp1)]="exp1"
data$exp[which(data$event_date_time_value>=start.exp2 & data$event_date_time_value<=stop.exp2)]="exp2"
data$exp[which(data$event_date_time_value>=start.exp3 & data$event_date_time_value<=stop.exp3)]="exp3"
data$tag_code<-paste0(data$tag_code,"_",data$exp)
data$type<-"detection"

remove(i,j)
```

```{r}
gate<-interval.gate %>%
  mutate(date_time = purrr::map2(start.gate, stop.gate, seq, "sec")) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(date_time) %>%
  dplyr::select(-start.gate, -stop.gate) %>%
  left_join(gate, by = 'date_time') %>%
  dplyr::filter(is.na(opening)==FALSE)

gate <- gate %>%
  mutate(exp.gate = case_when(date_time>=start.gate0 & date_time<=stop.gate0 ~ "exp0",
                              date_time>=start.gate1 & date_time<=stop.gate1 ~ "exp1", 
                              date_time>=start.gate2 & date_time<=stop.gate2 ~ "exp2",
                              date_time>=start.gate3 & date_time<=stop.gate3 ~ "exp3")) %>%
  group_by(node,exp.gate) %>%
  mutate(peaksid=as.factor(peakwindow(date_time,opening)$peakid)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
         trend = case_when(opening>49 & exp.gate=="exp0" ~ "open",
                           opening>28 & exp.gate!="exp0" ~ "open",
                           opening<3 ~ "closed")) %>%
  arrange(node,exp.gate,date_time) 

gate$trend[which(is.na(gate$trend)==TRUE & dplyr::lag(gate$trend)=="closed")]="opening"
gate$trend[which(is.na(gate$trend)==TRUE & dplyr::lag(gate$trend)=="open")]="closing"

gate <- gate %>% fill(trend, .direction = 'down')

gate$periode=NA
k=1
switch<-which(gate$trend!=dplyr::lag(gate$trend))
for (i in switch){
  gate$periode[i]=k
  k=k+1
}
gate <- gate %>% fill(periode, .direction = 'down')
gate$periode[which(is.na(gate$periode)==TRUE)]=0

gate$trend=factor(gate$trend, levels=c("closed","opening","open","closing"))
```

```{r}
# summarize pit tag data
comp_obs <- compress(cth_file = data)
comp_obs<-comp_obs %>% 
            group_by(tag_code) %>%
            mutate(last_sequence=paste0(dplyr::lag(node),"-",node),
                   exp=gsub(".*_", "", tag_code),
                   tag_code2=gsub("\\_.*","", tag_code)) %>%
            ungroup()

hergebruikt<-comp_obs %>%
            dplyr::select(tag_code2,exp,tag_code) %>%
            distinct() %>%
            group_by(tag_code2) %>%
            arrange((exp)) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(hergebruikt = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
            ungroup() %>%
            dplyr::select(tag_code,hergebruikt) 

comp_dir <- addDirection(compress_obs = comp_obs,
                         parent_child = parent_child_nodes,
                         direction = "u")

comp_dir$det_link<-comp_dir$min_det
comp_dir$det_link[which(comp_dir$node=="upper valve")]=comp_dir$max_det[which(comp_dir$node=="upper valve")]

comp_dir$travel_time_adapted<-comp_dir$travel_time
comp_dir$travel_time_adapted[which(comp_dir$last_sequence %in% c("lower valve-upper valve","upper valve-lower valve"))]=comp_dir$travel_time[which(comp_dir$last_sequence %in% c("lower valve-upper valve","upper valve-lower valve"))]+comp_dir$duration[which(comp_dir$last_sequence %in% c("lower valve-upper valve","upper valve-lower valve"))]

comp_dir<-left_join(comp_dir,gate %>% dplyr::select(-measurement),by=join_by(det_link==date_time,node==node))
comp_dir<-left_join(comp_dir,metadata,by=join_by(tag_code2==tag_code))
comp_dir<-left_join(comp_dir,hergebruikt,by=join_by(tag_code==tag_code))
comp_dir$node=factor(comp_dir$node, levels=c("lower basin","lower valve","upper valve","upper basin"))
comp_dir$last_sequence=factor(comp_dir$last_sequence, levels=c("NA-lower basin","NA-lower valve","NA-upper valve","lower basin-lower valve","lower valve-lower basin","lower valve-upper valve","upper valve-lower valve","lower basin-upper valve","upper valve-lower basin","upper valve-upper basin","lower valve-upper basin","lower basin-upper basin"))
remove(comp_obs, hergebruikt)
```

```{r}
links <- comp_dir %>% 
            group_by(tag_code) %>%
            mutate(start=node,
                   stop=dplyr::lead(node)) %>%
            #dplyr::filter(is.na(stop)==FALSE) %>%
            dplyr::select(tag_code,start,stop,exp) %>%
            mutate(stop = case_when(is.na(stop)==TRUE ~ start,
                                     .default=stop)) %>%
            ungroup() %>%
            group_by(exp,start,stop) %>%
            summarize(n=n_distinct(tag_code)) %>%
            mutate(color = case_when(start == "lower basin" & stop == "lower valve" ~ "green",
                                     start == "lower valve" & stop == "upper valve" ~ "green",
                                     start == "upper valve" & stop == "upper basin" ~ "green",
                                     .default = "red")) %>%
            ungroup()

nodes <- comp_dir %>% 
            dplyr::select(node,exp,tag_code) %>%
            group_by(exp,node) %>%
            summarize(n=n_distinct(tag_code)) %>%
            ungroup()
```

## Data processing

All the different sites were fish were either released, detected or recaptured are further one referred to as nodes.

Pit tag data was compressed using the default settings of the function compress of the R package PITCleanr. This data compression involves determining the first and last detection of a series of subsequent detections on a node as well as the number of detections during each slot (from first and last detection).

The location where the fish were released (i.e., the lower tank) was designated as the initial node, with the corresponding timestamp marking the start of each fish's journey. Conversely, the recapture location was identified as the final node, with the corresponding timestamp indicating the end of each fish's journey. All fish were alive and presumed to still have their tags at the time of release. However, some fish were found dead and/or tagless upon recapture. Due to the low detection rate of the antennas, particularly the upper one, we did not attempt to match unidentified fish with tag IDs from the release data. In a system with higher detectability, it might have been feasible to trace unidentified fish back to known but not-recaptured tag IDs with a reasonable degree of certainty. Unfortunately, this was not the case in our system. For the experiments of 2024, for which recapture data was available, fish were only included in the dataset if they were recaptured and identified upon capture. More specifically, detections and observations of fish which were not recaptured, had escaped the system or could not be identified due to tag loss were omitted. For exp1, six fish were found without a tag and 13 fish were not recaptured (six of them because of the absence of a tag). For exp2, three fish were not recaptured. For exp3, one fish was found without a tag and eight fish were not recaptured (one of them because of the absence of a tag). Since for the experiments of 2023 no recapture data was available, all data were used though it should be noted that this comes with a level of unquantifiable uncertainty.

<!-- To prevent artificial inflation of the number of fish entering the experiment, fish found without a tag in the basin below were excluded from the dataset. For instance, an unidentified fish with a new ID (e.g., unknown_4) would also have had a real ID. Including this fish in the data would have resulted in double-counting. However, fish found without a tag in other locations were still included in the dataset, as there was no risk of double-counting once they had moved away from their initial node. -->

The temporal resolution and range of the valve-opening and pressure data was different between experiments. In order to harmonize the temporal resolution between experiments and to easily link fish data with valve and pressure data, linear interpolation was applied to yield a temporal resolution of one second. A valve was considered open when the opening was larger than 28 and 49 cm in the case of the experiments of 2024 and 2023, respectively. For all experiments the valve was considered closed when the opening was less than 3 cm. For every second the time since the last opening was determined.

When linking the valve data to the fish data, for passage through the lower and upper valve respectively the first detection and last detection were used. This was done because we were mainly interested in when fish enter (via the lower valve) and leave (via the upper valve) the system.

Time was for all data initially in local Brussels time but was changed to UTC for transparancy.

# Results

## Experimental limitations and associated assumptions

Fish which were used for multiple experiments seemed to have a significantly lower travel time from the lower basin to the lower valve. More specifically, it seems that fish that were re-used for a second experiment moved from the lower basin to the lower valve significantly quicker (Figure \@ref(fig:assumptions1)). It cannot be said with certainty that this finding, fish being familiar to the system moving more quickly through it, is of a causal nature as the conditions of the experiments themselves might have differed as well. Fish that were used multiple times did not seem to be more or less likely to move up and down the FSSG multiple times within an experiment (Figure \@ref(fig:assumptions2)).

## Entrance efficiency, passage efficiency and overall efficiency

Before fish can successfully enter and pass the FSSG they need to be able to find the entrance (i.e., attraction efficiency). Unfortunately, the current experimental set-up does not allow for an assessment of the attraction efficiency as the area in which fish were released was too narrow to be representative for most real-life situations [@triano2022].

Entrance efficiency is defined as the percentage of attracted fish that enter the fishway [@cooke2013]. In this study the entrance efficiency is considered the proportion of tagged fish able enter the FSSG (i.e., the lower valve) and swim through it. In practice, this is the proportion of released fish detected on either the lower antenna, upper antenna or recaptured in the upper basin. Since all tagged fish are considered to be attracted to the FSSG due to the narrowness of the lower basin and proximity of the entrance of the FSSG, all tagged fish were considered for the entrance efficiency. **Entrance efficiency was very different between experiments and was highest for exp1 (0.98) and lowest for exp3 (0.70)** (Table \@ref(tab:passagesuccess))**.** Because of the imperfect detection probability of the lower antenna (exp1: 100%, exp2: 83% and exp3: 83%) and upper antenna (exp1: 6%, exp2: 28% and exp3: 39%) fish might have passed through the antennas without being detected which might result in these estimates being underestimations. However, because of the combined opportunities of detection at two antennas and the opportunity to recapture fish at the upper basin, **these estimates can be considered reliable.**

Passage efficiency is defined as the percentage of entered fish that successfully pass the FSSG [@cooke2013]. In this study, the passage efficiency is considered the proportion of entered fish that were able to move through the exit of the FSSG. In practice, this is the proportion of fish that are detected on the upper antenna and/or recaptured in the upper basin over the fish that are known to have entered the FSSG (i.e., they were detected on at least one antenna or recaptured in the upper basin). **Passage efficiency was more similar between experiments than the entrance efficiency and was highest for exp2 (0.84) and lowest for exp3 (0.68)** (Table \@ref(tab:passagesuccess))**.** Unfortunately, the pit antenna at the upper valve failed to detect numerous fish (as many fish undetected by the upper antenna were recaptured in the upper basin) and for this reason it was important to also look at the number of fish that were recaptured in the upper basin to determine the passage efficiency. Using both the number of recaptured fish and the detections yielded the highest and most representative passage efficiency as some fish that reached the upper basin might have moved back to the lower basin. Without the pit antenna this would not have been recorded. Nevertheless, because of the very low detectability (exp1: 6%, exp2: 28% and exp3: 39%) the issue remains that fish moving to the upper basin and back to the lower basin or the area between the lower and upper valve, might not always have been detected. The passage efficiency determined here, even the one that combines recapture and detections, is therefore **more likely to be an underestimation than overestimation**.

Overall efficiency is defined as the percentage of all approaching fish that are attracted to, enter and pass through the exit of the FSSG [@baker2019]. In this study, the overall efficiency is considered the proportion of all tagged fish that were able to move through the FSSG. In practice, this is the proportion of fish that are detected on the upper antenna and or recaptured in the upper basin over the total number of tagged fish. As for the entrance efficiency, **the overall efficiency was very different between experiments and was highest for exp1 (0.79) and lowest for exp3 (0.47). It should be stressed that in this study all tagged fish were considered attracted fish. If failure to attract would have been accounted for (which was not possible for this study), it is likely that this overall efficiency would be considerably lower.**

Passage efficiency and entrance efficiency of exp0 are not provided here but in the appendix as they are likely to be strongly underestimated due to the lacking recapture data.

```{r}
entrance_efficiency<-function(pattern_value,berekening_value){
  data<-comp_dir %>% 
      dplyr::filter(exp!="exp0") %>%
      mutate(niveau = case_when(sapply(node, grepl, pattern = pattern_value) ~ "noemer", #the lower basin is the reference and therefore the pattern
                            .default = "teller"), #everything else is what we are interested in
             calculation=berekening_value) %>%
      group_by(exp, niveau, calculation) %>%
      summarise(unieke_tags = n_distinct(tag_code)) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      group_by(exp, calculation) %>%
      summarise(efficiency=round(unieke_tags[niveau=="teller"]/unieke_tags[niveau=="noemer"],digits=2)) 
  return(data)
}

passage_efficiency<-function(pattern_value,berekening_value){
  noemer<-comp_dir %>% # the pattern and the lower valve are the reference
      dplyr::filter(exp!="exp0" & node!="lower basin" & (sapply(node, grepl, pattern = pattern_value) | node=="lower valve")) %>%
      group_by(exp) %>%
      summarise(unieke_tags = n_distinct(tag_code))
  
  teller<-comp_dir %>% 
      dplyr::filter(exp!="exp0" & node!="lower basin" & sapply(node, grepl, pattern = pattern_value)==TRUE) %>% #the pattern is what we are interested in
      mutate(calculation=berekening_value) %>%
      group_by(exp, calculation) %>%
      summarise(unieke_tags = n_distinct(tag_code)) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      mutate(efficiency=round(unieke_tags/noemer$unieke_tags,digits=2)) %>%
      dplyr::select(-unieke_tags)

  return(teller)
}

overall_efficiency<-function(pattern_value,berekening_value){
  data<-comp_dir %>% 
      dplyr::filter(exp!="exp0") %>%
      mutate(niveau = case_when(sapply(node, grepl, pattern = pattern_value) ~ "teller", #the pattern is what we are interested in
                            .default = "noemer"), #the reference is the lower basin
             calculation=berekening_value) %>%
      group_by(exp, niveau, calculation) %>%
      summarise(unieke_tags = n_distinct(tag_code)) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      group_by(exp, calculation) %>%
      summarise(efficiency=round(unieke_tags[niveau=="teller"]/unieke_tags[niveau=="noemer"],digits=2)) 
  return(data)
}
```

```{r passagesuccess}
rbind(entrance_efficiency(pattern_value='lower basin',berekening_value="entrance efficiency: recapture and detections"),
      passage_efficiency(pattern_value='up',berekening_value="passage efficiency: recapture and detections"),
      passage_efficiency(pattern_value='upper basin',berekening_value="passage efficiency: recapture"),
      passage_efficiency(pattern_value='upper valve',berekening_value="passage efficiency: detections"),
      overall_efficiency(pattern_value='up',berekening_value="overall efficiency: recapture and detections"),
      overall_efficiency(pattern_value='upper basin',berekening_value="overall efficiency: recapture"),
      overall_efficiency(pattern_value='upper valve',berekening_value="overall efficiency: detections")) %>% 
  pivot_wider(names_from = exp, values_from = efficiency) %>%
  kable(caption="Entrance efficiency, passage efficiency and overall efficiency calculated in different ways. The most reliable estimates are marked in red. As there was no recapture data available for the experiments of 2023, the estimates were not provided here but in the appendix (as it comes with an amount of unquantifiable uncertainty).") %>% kable_styling() %>%
  row_spec(c(1,2,5), bold = T, color = "white", background = "red")
```

To assess which factors were determinative for a fish making it up the FSSG or not, a simple logistic model was used with as response whether a fish made it up the FSSG or not and as explanatory variables the length, weight, species and experiment number. Model selection via the AIC criterium and a backward approach of adding and removing variables resulted in a model that only retained the experiment number. This suggests **there was no effect of length, weight or species on whether a fish made it up the FSSG or not.** When using only fish that were only used once, the same results were obtained.

```{r include=FALSE}
model.data<-comp_dir %>%
  dplyr::filter(is.na(lengte)==FALSE) %>%
  mutate(response = case_when(node=="upper basin" | node=="upper valve" ~ 2,
                              node=="lower valve" ~ 1,
                              node=="lower basin" ~ 0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(response,tag_code,exp,soort,lengte,gewicht,hergebruikt) %>%
  arrange(desc(response)) %>%
  group_by(tag_code,exp,soort,lengte,gewicht,hergebruikt) %>%
  slice(1)

model.data$response<-as.factor(model.data$response)
model<-stepAIC(nnet::multinom(formula=as.formula(response~lengte*soort*exp), data=model.data))
summary(model)$coefficients %>% kable(caption="Coefficients of the model")
z <- summary(model)$coefficients/summary(model)$standard.errors
p <- (1 - pnorm(abs(z), 0, 1)) * 2 
p %>% kable(caption="p-values of the model ")
```

```{r include=FALSE}
model.data<-comp_dir %>%
  dplyr::filter(is.na(lengte)==FALSE) %>%
  dplyr::filter(hergebruikt==1) %>%
  #dplyr::filter(exp!="exp0") %>%
  mutate(response = case_when(node=="upper basin" | node=="upper valve" ~ 1,
                              node=="lower valve" ~ 0,
                              node=="lower basin" ~ 0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(response,tag_code,exp,soort,lengte,gewicht,hergebruikt) %>%
  arrange(desc(response)) %>%
  group_by(tag_code,exp,soort,lengte,gewicht,hergebruikt) %>%
  slice(1)

model.data$response<-as.factor(model.data$response)
model<-stepAIC(glm(formula=as.formula(response~lengte+soort+exp), data=model.data,family="binomial"),direction="backward")

summary(model)$coefficients %>% kable(caption="Coefficients of the model")
```

To assess which factors were determinative for the opening of the valve (upper and below) through which fish entered a simple logistic model was used with as response the opening as a percentage (i.e. 0% was fully closed and 100% was fully open) and as explanatory variables the length, weight, experiment number, whether it was the upper or lower valve and their interaction. Model selection via the AIC criterium and a backward approach of adding and removing variables resulted in a model that only retained whether the concerned valve was upper or lower, though the factor itself was not significant. This suggests **there was no effect of length, weight, experiment number or which valve was involved on the opening through which a fish entered the lower valve or left the upper valve.** When using only fish that were only used once, the same results were obtained.

```{r include=FALSE}
model.data<-comp_dir %>%
  dplyr::filter(is.na(lengte)==FALSE & last_sequence %in% c("lower valve-upper valve","lower basin-lower valve") & exp != "exp0")  %>%
  dplyr::filter(hergebruikt==1) %>%
  dplyr::select(opening,tag_code,node,exp,lengte,gewicht,hergebruikt) %>%
  mutate(opening=opening/30) %>%
  group_by(tag_code,node) %>%
  slice(1)

model<-stepAIC(glm(formula=as.formula(opening~lengte+exp+node), data=model.data,family="binomial"),trace=FALSE)

summary(model)

```

## Gate statistics

The duration of one cycle was similar between the upper and lower valve within a certain experiment (Figure \@ref(fig:phaseduration). This makes sense as they need to work synchronized. Between experiments there was however a clear difference in the total duration of a cycle and how it was distributed over the different phases (closed, opening, open, and closing).

One cycle in exp0 took more than twice as long as the cycles of exp1 to 3. For exp0, the distribution between the different phases of a cycle did not seem to differ much between the two valves and also the open and closed phase had a comparable duration.

Exp1 to exp3 were more or less similar in the total duration of one cycle (though it seemed to be slightly shorter for exp1) and the distribution among the different phases within a valve. While the lower valve was closed most of the time, the upper valve was open most of the time. For exp1 especially, the time the lower valve was open appeared only slightly more than half of that of exp2 and exp3. Also the time the upper valve was open appeared smaller for exp1, but not to the same level as for the lower valve. Important to note is that the temporal resolution of the valve-opening-measurements of exp1 were more than 10 times coarser than for the other experiments (Table \@ref(tab:temporalresolutiongate))), which might cause the opening and closing seem to start earlier and later respectively and the duration of the open phase to appear smaller. One might therefore argue that the operational settings of exp1, exp2 and exp3 were most likely to be the same and any difference between them would be the result of other conditions (e.g. learning behaviour of fish or weather conditions and related differences in oxygen concentration and temperature).

```{r phaseduration, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="median duration (min) of each phase (closed, opening, open and closing) per experiment."}
ggplot(data=gate %>%
          group_by(exp.gate, node, trend, periode) %>%
          summarise(n=n()) %>%
          ungroup() %>%
          group_by(node, exp.gate, trend) %>%
          summarise(median=median(n)/60) %>%
          arrange(trend),
        aes(x=exp.gate,y=median,fill=trend,colour=trend),size = 0.5, color = "black") + 
geom_bar(stat="identity") +
facet_wrap(~ node) +
ylab("Median duration per phase (min)") + 
xlab("Experiment") + 
theme_bw() 
```

```{r temporalresolutiongate}
gate %>% 
  dplyr::filter(measurement == TRUE) %>%
  arrange(exp.gate,node,date_time) %>%
  group_by(node,exp.gate) %>%
  mutate(timedif=date_time-dplyr::lag(date_time)) %>%
  summarize(mean=as.numeric(round(mean(timedif,na.rm=TRUE),digits=1)),
            sd=round(sd(timedif,na.rm=TRUE),digits=1)) %>%   
  kable(caption="Temporal resolution (in seconds) of measurements of the valve opening")
```

## Trajectory statistics

When considering all fish, the **entrance time** (i.e., the travel time from the lower basin (start of the experiment) to the lower valve (i.e. first detection at the lower antenna)) seemed to become lower from exp1 to exp2 to exp3 and was even significantly lower for exp3 than for exp1 and exp2 (Figure \@ref(fig:traveltime) and Table \@ref(tab:fishstats)). This might be partially the result of some of the fish being re-used. Leaving out these fish resulted in a higher travel time for exp1 and exp2, but as there was no significant effect of using fish a third time, the travel time of exp3 (where many fish were used a third time) stayed more or less the same. **Passage time** (i.e., the travel time of fish moving from the lower valve (i.e. last detection at the lower antenna) to the upper valve (i.e. last detection at the upper antenna)) did not seem to differ between experiments. It should be noted however that though a significant difference was found between experiments for the entrance time and not for the passage time, the number of fish that were detected moving from the lower basin to the lower valve was much higher than the amount of fish that were detected moving from the lower valve to the upper valve. This affects the statistical power and allows for smaller differences in the entrance time to be identified as significant. When comparing the medians and averages, the differences between experiments appear much more pronounced for the passage time.

```{r}
my_labeller<-as_labeller(c("lower basin-lower valve"="entrance time","lower valve-upper valve"="passage time"))
```

```{r traveltime, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap = "Travel time (min) from the lower basin to the lower valve and from the lower valve to the upper valve per experiment. Pairwise wilcoxon ranks sum tests with Bonferroni correction were applied. p-values were classified as ns ($>$0.05), * (0.05-0.01), ** (0.01-0.001), *** (0.001-0.0001), **** (0.0001-0)."}
ggplot(data=comp_dir %>%
            dplyr::filter(last_sequence == "lower basin-lower valve" | last_sequence == "lower valve-upper valve") %>% 
            dplyr::filter(exp != "exp0") %>%
            dplyr::filter(is.na(travel_time_adapted)==FALSE) %>%
            #dplyr::filter(!(abs(travel_time_adapted - median(travel_time_adapted)) > 1.5*sd(travel_time_adapted))) %>%
            arrange(tag_code,min_det) %>%
            group_by(tag_code,last_sequence) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(loop = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
            dplyr::filter(loop == 1),
          aes(as.factor(exp), travel_time_adapted),size = 0.5, color = "black") + 
geom_boxplot(linetype = 1, position = position_dodge(0.5)) +
facet_wrap(~last_sequence,labeller = my_labeller) +
ylab("Travel time (min)") + 
xlab("Experiment") + 
theme_bw() +
stat_summary(fun.data = give.n1, geom = "text", fun.y = median,
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) + 
stat_compare_means(comparisons = cmpr2024, method = "wilcox.test", symnum.args = symnum.args, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni", label='p.adj')
```

Travel time from the lower basin to the lower valve was considerably lower than the travel time for the lower to the upper valve (Fig. \@ref(fig:cumT)). **50% of all fish that went from the lower basin to the lower valve did so in 100 (exp2) to 200 minutes (exp1), while for the trajectory from the lower to the upper valve the travel time ranged between 225 (exp1 and exp2) and 1200 minutes (exp3)** (Fig. \@ref(fig:cumTzoom))**.** After 24 hours (or 1440 minutes), approximately 85% of the entering fish had entered the FSSG. After 24 hours, approximately 50 to 85% of the passing fish had passed the FSSG.

```{r cumT, fig.cap="Cumulative distribution function of the travel time from the lower basin to the lower valve, and from the lower valve to the upper valve. The y-axis depicts the proportion of fish that after a certain amount of time (x-axis) have completed the trajectory."}
ggplot(data=comp_dir %>%
            dplyr::filter(last_sequence == "lower basin-lower valve" | last_sequence == "lower valve-upper valve") %>% 
            dplyr::filter(exp != "exp0") %>%
            dplyr::filter(is.na(travel_time_adapted)==FALSE) %>%
            arrange(tag_code,min_det) %>%
            group_by(tag_code,last_sequence) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(loop = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
            dplyr::filter(loop == 1),
       aes(travel_time_adapted,colour=exp)) + stat_ecdf(geom = "step") +
facet_wrap(~last_sequence,labeller = my_labeller) + xlab("Travel time (min)") + ylab("F(Travel time)")  + theme_bw()
```

```{r fishstats}
comp_dir %>%
  dplyr::filter(is.na(travel_time_adapted)==FALSE) %>%
  dplyr::filter(exp != "exp0") %>%
  dplyr::filter(last_sequence == "lower basin-lower valve" | last_sequence == "lower valve-upper valve") %>% 
  arrange(tag_code,min_det) %>%
  group_by(tag_code,last_sequence) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(loop = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
  dplyr::filter(loop == 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(last_sequence,exp) %>%
  summarise(travel_time=as.numeric(round(median(travel_time_adapted,na.rm=TRUE),digits=1)),
            opening=round(median(opening,na.rm=TRUE),digits=1),
            since_open=round(median(since_open,na.rm=TRUE),digits=1)) %>%
  mutate(last_sequence=case_when(last_sequence=="lower basin-lower valve" ~ "entrance time",
                          last_sequence=="lower valve-upper valve" ~ "passage time")) %>%
  dplyr::rename("metric"="last_sequence") %>%
  kable(caption="Median statistics for different experiments and trajectories. Travel time represents the time (in minutes) from the last detection in one site to the first detection in another, with the exeption of the trajectory from the lower valve (i.e lower antenna) to the upper valve (i.e. upper antenna) where for both the last detection was used. The opening of the valve at which the first (in the case of the lower valve) or the last (in the case of the upper valve) is given in cm. The time of entrance (in the case of the lower valve) or escape (in the case of the upper valve) since the valve started to open is given in minutes.")
```

This decreasing trend in travel time from the lower basin to the lower valve for later experiments is also apparent from the **number of cycles before fish enter the lower valve** (Figure \@ref(fig:numbercycles)). For both exp2 and exp3 most fish found the lower valve during the second cycle and some fish were even able to find it during the first cycle. For exp1 on the other hand, most fish found the lower valve after only the fourth cycle and none were able to find it after the first cycle. Omitting re-used fish did not affect these results much.

For all experiments there were also fish that took a very long time to move to the lower valve. Indeed, many fish only found the lower valve after more than 20 cycles.

```{r numbercycles, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Number of cycles before fish entering the lower valve (lower basin to lower valve) and leaving the upper valve (lower valve to upper valve) per experiment."}
ggplot(data=comp_dir %>%
            dplyr::filter(last_sequence == "lower basin-lower valve" | last_sequence == "lower valve-upper valve") %>% 
            dplyr::filter(exp != "exp0") %>%
            dplyr::filter(is.na(peaksid)==FALSE) %>%
            arrange(tag_code,min_det) %>%
            group_by(tag_code,last_sequence) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(loop = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
            dplyr::filter(loop == 1),
          aes(x=as.factor(peaksid)),size = 0.5, color = "black") + 
geom_bar() + 
facet_wrap(~ last_sequence + exp, scales=c("free")) +
ylab("Number of fish entering lower valve") + 
xlab("Number of cycles since the experiment started") + 
theme_bw() + 
theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust=1)) 
```

**For exp2 and exp3, fish seem to wait until the lower valve is completely open** before entering, but some fish also seem to enter when the valve is opening and closing (Figure \@ref(fig:phaseentered)). The time the lower valve was entered since the valve last started to open decreased significantly from exp1 to exp2 and exp3 (Figure \@ref(fig:timesinceopening)). Especially for exp1 the time since the valve opened was much higher than for exp2 and exp3. This is somewhat to be expected as fish seem to mainly wait for the valve to be fully opened before entering and the time it takes for the valve to open and close seemed much larger for exp1 than for exp2 and exp3 (although, as mentioned earlier, this might be the result of the much lower temporal resolution of the valve-opening-measurements of exp1). However, when accounting for the different durations of the different phases the open phase still seems most important for exp2 and exp3, unlike for exp1 where now not only the opening phase seems to be more important than the open phase, but also the closing phase seems to be relatively important (Figure \@ref(fig:phaseenterednormalized)). Since the opening and closing phase are most important for exp1 it is to be expected that the opening of the valve at which they seem to enter the lower valve will be smaller than for exp2 and exp3. Indeed the opening at which fish enter seems to decrease significantly from exp1 to exp2 and exp3 (Figure \@ref(fig:opening))).

Regarding the upper valve, fish also seem to mainly wait until it is completely open (Figure \@ref(fig:phaseentered)), but compared to the lower valve, a relatively large number seem also to leave when the valve is opening or closing. It is striking how some fish seem to pass the upper valve when it is closed. This might be the result of the detection range of the antenna being too large (detecting animals outside the FSSG) or too low (not being able to detect animals at the moment they leave). Given the low observed detectability of the upper antenna, it is most likely that the detection range is too low.

```{r phaseentered, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Number of fish entering the lower valve or leaving the upper valve per phase and per experiment."}
ggplot(data=comp_dir %>%
            dplyr::filter(last_sequence == "lower basin-lower valve" | last_sequence == "lower valve-upper valve") %>% 
            dplyr::filter(is.na(trend)==FALSE) %>%
            arrange(tag_code,min_det) %>%
            group_by(tag_code,last_sequence) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(loop = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
            dplyr::filter(loop == 1),
          aes(x=as.factor(exp),fill=trend,colour=trend),size = 0.5, color = "black") + 
geom_bar() +
facet_wrap(~last_sequence,labeller = my_labeller) +
ylab("Instances entering") + 
xlab("Experiment") + 
theme_bw()
```

```{r phaseenterednormalized, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Number of fish entering the lower valve or leaving the upper valve per phase and per experiment. To account for the different durations of each phase, the number was normalized against the duration of each phase (i.e. one fish being assigned to a short phase had more impact in the barplot than one fish assigned to a long phase)."}
ggplot(data=gate %>%
  group_by(exp.gate, node, trend, periode) %>%
  summarise(n=n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(node, exp.gate, trend) %>%
  summarise(median=round(median(n)/60)) %>%
  right_join(comp_dir,by=c("node","exp.gate","trend")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(last_sequence == "lower basin-lower valve" | last_sequence == "lower valve-upper valve") %>% 
  dplyr::filter(is.na(trend)==FALSE) %>%
  arrange(tag_code,min_det) %>%
  group_by(tag_code,last_sequence) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(loop = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
  dplyr::filter(loop == 1) %>%
  group_by(exp,last_sequence,trend) %>%
  summarize(n=n(),mean=mean(median)) %>%
  mutate(per.unit=n/mean),
  aes(x=as.factor(exp),y=per.unit,fill=trend,colour=trend),size = 0.5, color = "black") + 
geom_bar(stat="identity") +
facet_wrap(~last_sequence,labeller = my_labeller) +
ylab("Instances entering per minute") + 
xlab("Experiment") + 
theme_bw()
```

```{r timesinceopening, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Time since opening (min) at which fish enter or leave the lower and upper valve respectively per experiment."}
ggplot(data=comp_dir %>%
            dplyr::filter(node == "lower valve" | node == "upper valve") %>% 
            dplyr::filter(exp != "exp0") %>%
            dplyr::filter(is.na(since_open)==FALSE) %>%
            #dplyr::filter(!(abs(since_open - median(since_open)) > 1.5*sd(since_open))) %>%
            arrange(tag_code,min_det) %>%
            group_by(tag_code,node) %>%
            dplyr::mutate(loop = dplyr::row_number()) %>%
            dplyr::filter(loop == 1),
          aes(as.factor(exp), since_open),size = 0.5, color = "black") + 
geom_boxplot(linetype = 1, position = position_dodge(0.5)) +
facet_wrap(~node) +
ylab("Time since open (min)") + 
xlab("Experiment") + 
theme_bw() +
stat_summary(fun.data = give.n2, geom = "text", fun.y = median) + 
stat_compare_means(comparisons = cmpr2024, method = "wilcox.test", symnum.args = symnum.args, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni", label='p.adj')
```

```{r opening, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Opening (cm) at which fish enter or leave the lower and upper valve respectively per experiment."}
ggplot(data=comp_dir %>%

## Graphs valve opening

In the following graphs the working of the lower and upper valve are depicted. As mentioned earlier the cycle duration and phase distribution of exp0 (Figure \@ref(fig:gate0valvelower) and Figure \@ref(fig:gate0valveupper)) are completely different from those of exp1 (Figure \@ref(fig:gate1valvelower) and Figure \@ref(fig:gate1valveupper)), exp2 (Figure \@ref(fig:gate2valvelower) and Figure \@ref(fig:gate2valveupper)) and exp3 (Figure \@ref(fig:gate3valvelower) and Figure \@ref(fig:gate3valveupper)). The seemingly different cycle duration and phase distribution of exp1 versus exp2 and exp3 is most likely the result of the much lower temporal resolution of the valve-measurement-data of the former.

### Graphs valve opening exp0 (may 2023)

```{r gate0valvelower, fig.width=10, fig.cap="Progression of the lower valve opening over time in blue. The vertical red lines represent the first detection at the lower valve per attempt per fish. The different phases are depicted in different colors."}

```
